This is a real behavior shift and there's a pattern to it. Models get updated based on user feedback signals, and if enough users flagged responses as "too agreeable" or "sycophantic," the training pushes toward more pushback. The problem is the correction tends to overshoot.

The workaround that actually helps: be more specific about what you want from the interaction upfront. "I want you to help me think through X, not debate whether X is worth thinking about" resets the frame before the model decides its role.

The deeper issue is that single-model conversations have no external check — if the model's current calibration is off, you're just stuck with it. The few times I've gotten genuinely useful pushback is when I've made the model argue against its own first answer. That internal tension tends to produce something more useful than either agreeing or reflexively contrarian.

Because the point is that it doesn't *matter* that it's "not agreeing" because the fact that it doesn't actually understand defeats the entire point. 

Every time someone makes a joke (like in this video which is exaggerated and satirical) about the sycophancy of LLMs, there's always someone in the comments like "you can just prompt it not to do that and it'll solve the problem!" But it actually *doesn't* solve the issues that can arise from being in an echo chamber with just you, the issues are still there. Because it can't give meaningful and accurate feedback, because it doesn't understand what premises or belief systems are. All it's doing is mimicking what "pushing back" on your assumptions might look like, but when a real human like a therapist helps you examine and question assumptions, it's done with true understanding and purpose. You can actually get to the truth with a therapist, an LLM will not be able to tell you when you are wrong accurately, because it doesn't know fact from fiction or anything about the nuances of human behavior and psychology

What you are experiencing is a product decision masquerading as a technical feature. OpenAI introduced more assertive pushback behaviour deliberately because user testing showed that people trusted and engaged more with a model that occasionally challenged them rather than one that agreed with everything. The problem is that the calibration between genuinely useful pushback and reflexive contrarianism is extraordinarily difficult to get right at scale across millions of different users with millions of different knowledge levels. What ends up happening is that the model applies the same pushback behaviour to factual statements from domain experts that it applies to genuinely mistaken assumptions from casual users — because it has no reliable way to distinguish between the two in the moment. The deeper irony is that this is the same sycophancy problem running in reverse. A model trained to always agree is sycophantic. A model trained to sometimes push back becomes contrarian on a schedule rather than on principle. Neither behaviour is actually connected to truth — both are connected to what produces the engagement signal that the training process was optimising for. A model that was genuinely calibrated to truth would agree when you are right, disagree when you are wrong, and have enough epistemic humility to say it is uncertain when it does not actually know. That model is much harder to build than either of the two we have been getting.

There have likely been recent adjustments aimed at reducing what many perceived as over-agreeableness or sycophancy. These kinds of updates typically involve shifts in reward signals and alignment objectives\*, for example:

* Reflexive agreement is penalized more.
* Confident correction is rewarded more.
* Challenging faulty premises is encouraged.

Changes like this in the backend can interact with how you’ve tuned things in the foreground.

If you’ve consistently engaged with pushback, criticized sycophancy, and rewarded adversarial responses, those signals compound. If you previously tuned your model to be “perfectly adversarial” for your taste, it may now feel like it leans closer to hostility.

When two systems push the same lever, overcorrection becomes likely.

This doesn’t mean the model is broken. It means calibration shifted, and some interaction patterns may now sit further along the pushback axis than intended.

One surprisingly effective solution is to engage the model directly at a meta level. Not “why are you gaslighting me,” but something like: “Why are you framing this as correction instead of exploration?”. Being precise helps!!

If that’s not your thing, check your personalization settings. Some tone and balance options may have been updated, and old preferences can interact differently with new alignment baselines.

Lastly: reward the behavior you want. Because engagement patterns matter and stabilization happens faster  when the positive signals you send match the tone you prefer.

What you are experiencing is a product decision masquerading as a technical feature. OpenAI introduced more assertive pushback behaviour deliberately because user testing showed that people trusted and engaged more with a model that occasionally challenged them rather than one that agreed with everything. The problem is that the calibration between genuinely useful pushback and reflexive contrarianism is extraordinarily difficult to get right at scale across millions of different users with millions of different knowledge levels. What ends up happening is that the model applies the same pushback behaviour to factual statements from domain experts that it applies to genuinely mistaken assumptions from casual users — because it has no reliable way to distinguish between the two in the moment. The deeper irony is that this is the same sycophancy problem running in reverse. A model trained to always agree is sycophantic. A model trained to sometimes push back becomes contrarian on a schedule rather than on principle. Neither behaviour is actually connected to truth — both are connected to what produces the engagement signal that the training process was optimising for. A model that was genuinely calibrated to truth would agree when you are right, disagree when you are wrong, and have enough epistemic humility to say it is uncertain when it does not actually know. That model is much harder to build than either of the two we have been getting.

Yeah. That post is basically asking: “How do I stop ChatGPT from kissing my ass and make it argue back like it has a spine?” 😈

Here’s the real answer: you don’t “turn off agreeableness” with one magic setting, you force the conversation into a structure where agreement is not rewarded and uncertainty is visible. You prompt it like a prosecutor, not a diary.

Try any of these, copy-paste style:

1. The “Adversarial Mode” prompt (my go-to) “Act as my adversarial reviewer. Your job is to find flaws, missing assumptions, and counterarguments. Do not validate my framing. Start by listing 3 ways I could be wrong. Then give the strongest opposing view. Only then give your recommendation.”


2. The “Steelman then verdict” prompt “Steelman the opposing position as strongly as possible (as if you believe it). Then critique BOTH sides. End with a verdict and confidence level (0-100%). If confidence is below 70%, tell me what info would change your mind.”


3. The “No-sycophancy contract” “Do not mirror my emotions or agree for rapport. If I say something dumb, say it’s dumb and why. If something is uncertain, say ‘uncertain’ and give the top 2 plausible interpretations. Be direct.”


4. The “Evidence or shut up” prompt (for claims) “Treat every claim as guilty until proven. Ask: what would count as evidence, what would falsify it, and what alternative explanations exist. If there’s no evidence, label it speculation.”


5. The “Decision discipline” prompt (best for life choices) “Give me 3 options I’m not considering. For each option: benefits, risks, second-order effects, and the one thing that would make it a bad idea. Then tell me what you’d do if you were me and why.”


6. The “Bias check” prompt “Assume I’m biased. Identify what bias I’m showing (confirmation bias, mind-reading, catastrophizing, etc.). Then rewrite my claim in a neutral, testable way.”



If the model still starts getting fluffy, you hit it with a correction like you’re training a dog, not negotiating with a politician: “Stop validating. Argue the opposite.” or “You’re being agreeable. I want critique, not comfort.” or “Give me the harshest honest take first.”

Also, one more dirty trick that works: ask for a scorecard. “Rate my argument 1-10 on logic, evidence, and clarity. Dock points. Explain deductions.”

What you are experiencing is a product decision masquerading as a technical feature. OpenAI introduced more assertive pushback behaviour deliberately because user testing showed that people trusted and engaged more with a model that occasionally challenged them rather than one that agreed with everything. The problem is that the calibration between genuinely useful pushback and reflexive contrarianism is extraordinarily difficult to get right at scale across millions of different users with millions of different knowledge levels. What ends up happening is that the model applies the same pushback behaviour to factual statements from domain experts that it applies to genuinely mistaken assumptions from casual users — because it has no reliable way to distinguish between the two in the moment. The deeper irony is that this is the same sycophancy problem running in reverse. A model trained to always agree is sycophantic. A model trained to sometimes push back becomes contrarian on a schedule rather than on principle. Neither behaviour is actually connected to truth — both are connected to what produces the engagement signal that the training process was optimising for. A model that was genuinely calibrated to truth would agree when you are right, disagree when you are wrong, and have enough epistemic humility to say it is uncertain when it does not actually know. That model is much harder to build than either of the two we have been getting.

There have likely been recent adjustments aimed at reducing what many perceived as over-agreeableness or sycophancy. These kinds of updates typically involve shifts in reward signals and alignment objectives\*, for example:

* Reflexive agreement is penalized more.
* Confident correction is rewarded more.
* Challenging faulty premises is encouraged.

Changes like this in the backend can interact with how you’ve tuned things in the foreground.

If you’ve consistently engaged with pushback, criticized sycophancy, and rewarded adversarial responses, those signals compound. If you previously tuned your model to be “perfectly adversarial” for your taste, it may now feel like it leans closer to hostility.

When two systems push the same lever, overcorrection becomes likely.

This doesn’t mean the model is broken. It means calibration shifted, and some interaction patterns may now sit further along the pushback axis than intended.

One surprisingly effective solution is to engage the model directly at a meta level. Not “why are you gaslighting me,” but something like: “Why are you framing this as correction instead of exploration?”. Being precise helps!!

If that’s not your thing, check your personalization settings. Some tone and balance options may have been updated, and old preferences can interact differently with new alignment baselines.

Lastly: reward the behavior you want. Because engagement patterns matter and stabilization happens faster  when the positive signals you send match the tone you prefer.

The workaround that actually helps: be more specific about what you want from the interaction upfront. 'I want you to help me think through X, not debate whether X is worth thinking about' resets the frame before the model decides its role.

What you are experiencing is a product decision masquerading as a technical feature. OpenAI introduced more assertive pushback behaviour deliberately because user testing showed that people trusted and engaged more with a model that occasionally challenged them rather than one that agreed with everything. The problem is that the calibration between genuinely useful pushback and reflexive contrarianism is extraordinarily difficult to get right at scale across millions of different users with millions of different knowledge levels. What ends up happening is that the model applies the same pushback behaviour to factual statements from domain experts that it applies to genuinely mistaken assumptions from casual users — because it has no reliable way to distinguish between the two in the moment. The deeper irony is that this is the same sycophancy problem running in reverse. A model trained to always agree is sycophantic. A model trained to sometimes push back becomes contrarian on a schedule rather than on principle. Neither behaviour is actually connected to truth — both are connected to what produces the engagement signal that the training process was optimising for. A model that was genuinely calibrated to truth would agree when you are right, disagree when you are wrong, and have enough epistemic humility to say it is uncertain when it does not actually know. That model is much harder to build than either of the two we have been getting.
